brief.objective: How should Oatly grow profitably in the United States over the next 24 months? Which channels, customer segments and product bets should it prioritise?
brief.targetMarket: US plant-based dairy alternatives (oat milk and adjacent categories), across retail and foodservice
brief.constraints: No major capital expenditure on new US production capacity. Gross margin must improve. Marketing budget roughly flat year over year.
brief.notes: Management wants to protect the coffee-shop (barista) franchise while finding a scalable retail growth engine. The board is sceptical of launching many new SKUs.

plan.objective: Decide where Oatly should concentrate US commercial effort over the next 24 months — which channels (retail vs foodservice), customer segments and product/SKU bets — to deliver profitable growth without new US capex, with improving gross margin and flat marketing spend.
keyQuestions: Is the US oat milk category still growing, flat or declining in volume and value, and where is growth shifting (creamers, barista, other plant bases, whole-milk-style blends)?
Which channels (grocery, club, convenience, coffee chains, independent cafés, foodservice distribution) offer the best margin-adjusted growth for Oatly?
Which customer segments (coffee-led household, mainstream dairy-switching, value-seeking, foodservice operators) can be won with flat marketing spend?
What are Oatly's current US gross margin drivers and levers (mix, pricing/promo depth, co-manufacturing, freight, SKU rationalisation)?
Where are competitors (Chobani, Califia, Silk/Danone, Planet Oat, private label) taking share and on what price points?
Which product adjacencies have proven US velocity and better margin than core oat milk?

summary.text: US retail plant-based milk is a $2.7 billion category that declined 2% in dollars and 5% in units in 2025, and holds 13% of total milk dollar sales.
Oat milk is the second-largest base at 21% of plant-based milk unit share, behind almond at 49%.
Category decline is driven by distribution losses rather than weakening demand per store: dollar velocity rose 4% and unit velocity 3% in conventional multi-outlet, and 3%/2% in natural.
Oatly is outgrowing the category in North America, with Q2 2026 revenue of $66.9 million, up 5.9% on +1.9% volume and +4.0% price/mix, and Q1 2026 retail sales up 10% against a 3% oat milk decline.
Growth in the wider plant-based set has shifted to adjacencies — RTD beverages (double-digit), bars (16%), yogurt (7% dollars), creamer (2%) — rather than to base milk.
Third-party US oat milk market sizings disagree by roughly 2x ($860 million in 2025 versus $1.67 billion in 2025), so they should not be used as a planning base without reconciliation.

options.title: Barista Bridge: make the café franchise the engine of retail distribution
options.summary: Treat the coffee-shop business as a marketing asset rather than a volume engine, and convert café-built habit into retail volume on the existing Barista platform. Defend and diversify foodservice (more independents and distributor-served accounts, less dependence on the single largest customer), then push Barista and core oatmilk into more doors — club, natural and mainstream refrigerated shelf — rather than onto more shelf facings of new products. Growth comes from distribution and velocity on SKUs that already exist, which fits the no-capex, flat-marketing and SKU-sceptical constraints, and mirrors the Europe & International playbook where a 77% retail mix grew volume 16.9% led by Barista.

benefits.text: Europe & International grew volume 16.9% in Q2 2026 led by Barista products with a 77% retail mix, providing an internal precedent for a Barista-led retail engine.
Category decline is driven by distribution losses while velocities rose (dollar +4%, unit +3% in conventional multi-outlet), so winning doors is the highest-return lever available.

Oatly's US retail channel is already the growth driver: retail rose to 63% of North America revenue in Q2 2026 from 59%, Q1 2026 retail sales grew 10% against a 3% oat milk category decline, and the Q2 volume increase was mainly retail-driven.
Coffee remains the strongest demand anchor for oat milk, with 33% of US coffee orders containing it, and management identifies foodservice as where habits are created.
It directly answers both management asks: protect the barista franchise and find a scalable retail engine, without the new-SKU load the board resists.

Higher volume through existing co-manufacturing and optimised facilities extends the fixed-cost-absorption benefit that added 210 basis points to Q2 2026 gross margin, so margin can improve without capex.

risks.text: The out-of-home base is shrinking: US restaurants serving alternative milks fell 8.1% to about 103,900 locations, so foodservice defence may hold share in a declining location pool.

Concentration risk is real but unquantified: prior-year North America declines were driven mainly by sourcing changes and the segment's largest customer, and excluding that customer Q1 2026 revenue grew 12.3%.

Winning mainstream doors invites direct price competition from Planet Oat, which competes aggressively on price in conventional grocery, at a time when plant-based milk still costs over twice conventional milk.
Distribution gains normally require trade spend and slotting, which compresses net revenue per litre even when gross margin percentage holds.
More evidence needed: Oatly's US ACV and points of distribution by channel are not disclosed, so the size of the remaining door-level white space cannot be quantified.

requirements.text: Capability: a retail distribution and category-management function able to win and hold shelf in club, natural and mainstream refrigerated sets, where refrigerated formats are 88% of plant-based milk dollars.
Partner: continued reliance on co-manufacturers under the stated asset-light model to absorb incremental retail volume without new US plants.
Partner: foodservice distributors already carrying the foodservice-friendly Barista SKU, used to broaden the independent-café base away from single-customer dependence.

Investment: reallocation of the roughly flat marketing budget from broad awareness toward café-to-home conversion and in-store visibility, rather than incremental spend; group SG&A already rose $10.6 million in Q2 2026 partly on branding and distribution costs.
Time: distribution resets in club, natural and grocery follow annual or semi-annual shelf review cycles, so the 24-month window realistically allows two resets.
Investment: no incremental capex beyond the existing $20–30 million group guidance range.

options.title: Own the Coffee Occasion: a focused premium adjacency portfolio
options.summary: Shift the unit of competition from the milk carton to the coffee occasion, and monetise it through higher-price-per-litre formats: flavoured creamers, matcha and RTD coffee drinks, and flavour-first barista variants, supported by branded partnerships such as Nespresso. The logic is to escape a declining base-milk category by following the growth — plant-based RTD beverages grew double digits and creamer households repeat at 65% — and to lift gross margin through mix rather than volume. This requires accepting a small number of new SKUs against board scepticism, and defending them with distribution discipline rather than breadth.

benefits.text: Growth in plant-based has moved to adjacencies: RTD beverages grew double digits in dollars and units in 2025, bars 16% in dollars, yogurt 7%, and creamer 2% in both dollars and units.
Cross-purchase makes the adjacency route efficient: 25% of plant-based milk households already buy plant-based creamer versus 14% of all households, and creamer repeat is 65%.
Oatly already has the launch base: creamers are distributed nationally at $5.99 suggested retail, and matcha RTD and flavoured barista options have been unveiled in the US.
SPINS expects plant-based innovation to concentrate in RTD beverages and snacking because consumers prefer low-stakes trial, aligning the bet with where trial is happening.
Higher-value formats support price/mix, which contributed 4.0 percentage points of Oatly's 5.9% North America revenue growth in Q2 2026 and is the CEO's stated strategic axis.
The Nespresso partnership's second chapter gives a branded at-home iced-coffee platform without buying media.

risks.text: It runs against the board's stated scepticism about launching many new SKUs, so approval and internal sponsorship are uncertain.
New formats typically need launch marketing, which is hard to fund with a roughly flat budget while group SG&A is already rising on branding and distribution costs.
Conventional creamer is outgrowing plant-based creamer (4% versus 2% dollar growth), so the adjacency is contested by dairy incumbents.
Califia has already moved on the out-of-home pouring occasion by acquiring the Uproot self-serve dispenser brand, and Starbucks has launched its own oat-milk non-dairy creamer.
New formats may require co-manufacturing capability Oatly does not have in the US, and RTD in particular is being launched abroad first (Tesco UK), suggesting US supply is not yet proven at scale.
More evidence needed: no SKU-level profitability for Oatly's US portfolio, so it cannot be shown that creamer or RTD carries better margin than core oatmilk.

requirements.text: Capability: an innovation-to-shelf process that can limit the bet to a small number of coffee-occasion SKUs and kill underperformers quickly, given board SKU scepticism.
Partner: co-manufacturers able to produce RTD and creamer formats in the US under the asset-light model, since no new US capacity is permitted.
Partner: continuation and US extension of the Nespresso relationship as a low-media route to the coffee occasion.
Investment: launch funding reallocated from core-brand media rather than added, to hold marketing roughly flat.
Time: at least two shelf-reset cycles within 24 months to build distribution and read repeat rates before scaling.

options.title: Margin First: prune the tail and harvest premium channels
options.summary: Make gross margin and cash the primary objective and accept slower top-line growth. Extend the mix management that already added 110 basis points of gross margin by deliberately reducing sales to lower-margin products and customers, rationalising the SKU tail, and concentrating volume on the highest-margin channels and accounts — natural, club and premium independent cafés — where plant-based already holds outsized share and shoppers tolerate a premium. The logic is that with $517.8 million of debt, $44.6 million of cash and negative first-half free cash flow, the binding constraint is profitability, not share.

benefits.text: The approach is already proven inside the business: pricing and product mix added 110 basis points to gross margin as Oatly reduced sales of lower-margin products and customers and increased higher-margin ones.
Group gross margin reached 33.9% in Q2 2026, up 143 basis points, with North America channel mix explicitly cited as a driver — evidence that mix discipline works in this market.

It addresses the balance sheet directly: $44.6 million cash against $517.8 million debt and a $12.3 million first-half free cash outflow, with the restructuring programme targeting $35–45 million of annual savings.
Premium channels are structurally favourable: plant-based milk is 30% of total milk sales in the natural channel, and plant-based households skew to incomes over $100K and post-college education.
Fewest new SKUs of any option, which matches board preference and reduces complexity cost.

risks.text: Deliberate volume reduction works against the fixed-cost absorption that delivered a 210 basis point gross margin benefit from higher throughput, so margin gains could partly self-cancel.
Guidance has been raised to +8% to +10% constant-currency revenue growth, so a harvest posture in North America would sit awkwardly with external expectations.
Ceding mainstream doors accelerates the distribution loss that is already driving category decline, and hands shelf to Planet Oat on price and Silk on distribution and protein.
Premium positioning is exposed to the price barrier: plant-based milk prices rose 2% in 2025 while units fell 5%, and the category still costs over twice conventional milk.
Narrowing to premium channels shrinks the funnel that counters lapsing, in a category where 83% of US plant-based milk consumers report switching back to dairy.
More evidence needed: Oatly does not disclose North America gross margin or SKU-level profitability, so the size of the prunable low-margin tail cannot be sized externally.

requirements.text: Capability: customer- and SKU-level profitability reporting for North America good enough to decide what to exit, which is not visible in public disclosure.
Capability: commercial willingness to walk away from named low-margin customers, extending the sourcing and customer changes that already reduced North America revenue 6.8% in Q2 2025.
Investment: minimal incremental spend; marketing held flat and skewed to owned channels and natural/club shopper programmes.
Partner: renegotiated co-manufacturing terms to protect unit economics at lower throughput under the asset-light model.
Time: visible within four quarters, since mix actions show up in the gross margin bridge within a quarter or two as they did in Q2 2025 and Q2 2026.

recommendation.headline: Run the Barista Bridge: defend and diversify the café franchise, and grow US retail by winning doors and velocity on existing Barista and core SKUs rather than by launching a new portfolio.

rationale.text: The evidence points to distribution, not demand, as the binding category problem: plant-based sales fell on distribution losses while dollar velocity rose 4% and unit velocity 3% in conventional multi-outlet.

Oatly's own numbers show the retail engine already working against a declining category — retail up to 63% of North America revenue, Q1 2026 retail sales up 10% versus a 3% oat milk decline, and Q2 volume growth mainly retail-driven.
Europe & International demonstrates the same logic at scale: 16.9% volume growth led by Barista in a 77% retail mix, which is the closest available proof that a Barista-led retail push can work.

The coffee occasion is the one position competitors are not attacking head-on, with 33% of US coffee orders containing oat milk and Oatly positioned on barista-channel dominance while rivals compete on price, protein and distribution scale.

It fits all three constraints: incremental volume flows through co-manufacturers under the asset-light model rather than new capex, extends the 210 basis point fixed-cost absorption benefit, and leans on café-built habit instead of incremental media.
It also satisfies the two client mandates simultaneously — protecting the barista franchise and supplying a scalable retail engine — without the SKU proliferation the board resists.

Diversifying foodservice toward distributor-served independents is the practical hedge against single-customer concentration, since excluding the largest foodservice customer Q1 2026 North America revenue grew 12.3%.

whyNotOthers.text: Option B chases faster-growing adjacencies such as double-digit RTD, but it requires new SKUs the board resists and launch funding that a roughly flat marketing budget cannot supply, and no SKU-level profitability data exists to prove the margin case — it is better sequenced as a two-to-three-SKU coffee-occasion test inside Option A once retail doors are secured.

Option C would improve margin percentage through mix pruning, but deliberately shedding volume undercuts the fixed-cost absorption that delivered 210 basis points of gross margin and accelerates the distribution loss already driving category decline, while sitting against raised guidance of +8% to +10% constant-currency growth.

conditionsToRevisit.text: Shift toward Option C if North America Adjusted EBITDA falls back below breakeven from the $0.7 million achieved in Q2 2026, or if group gross margin gives back the 143 basis point gain.
Shift toward Option B if Oatly's own US creamer and matcha RTD lines show repeat rates near the 65% plant-based creamer benchmark while core oatmilk retail velocity stalls.
Reassess the foodservice defence if US locations serving alternative milks keep falling at the 8.1% annual rate, or if the largest foodservice customer's contract changes materially.

Reassess pricing posture if unit declines steepen beyond 2025's 5% while average plant-based milk prices keep rising, indicating the premium is no longer sustainable against Planet Oat-style value competition.
Reassess the product line if Silk Protein-style nutrition claims visibly take share, given protein and whole-ingredient positioning is the 2026 innovation axis amid ultra-processed backlash.
Reassess supply strategy if expanded third-party capacity such as SunOpta's 60%-plus Modesto increase drives private-label share gains that erode Oatly's shelf economics.

Commission brand-level US oat milk share tracking, US ACV by channel and a North America SKU profitability view before committing the second year of spend; these are the gaps that most constrain this decision.

businessCase.summary: The Barista Bridge grows US revenue by winning distribution and velocity for existing Barista and core oatmilk SKUs, while defending and de-concentrating the coffee-shop franchise. It needs no new US capacity, holds marketing roughly flat by reallocating spend from broad awareness to café-to-home conversion and shelf visibility, and improves gross margin mainly through fixed-cost absorption on higher throughput plus channel mix. Base case: North America revenue rises from an annualised ~$258M to ~$292M within 24 months, with North America Adjusted EBITDA exiting at roughly $13M annualised. The case is funded by reallocation and trade investment, not capex.

risksToCase.text: The North America Adjusted EBITDA baseline is annualised from a single quarter of $0.7M, so the profit projection is highly sensitive to seasonality and to one weak quarter.

Foodservice concentration is unquantified: prior-year North America declines were driven mainly by sourcing changes and the segment's largest customer, and loss of that account could erase the base case foodservice assumption.
The out-of-home pool is shrinking, with US restaurants serving alternative milks down 8.1% to about 103,900 locations, so foodservice may decline even with successful independent-café wins.
Category units are falling faster than dollars (plant-based milk -5% units, -2% dollars, with average prices up 2%), so a volume-and-doors strategy runs against the prevailing trend.

Mainstream door wins invite price competition from Planet Oat, which competes aggressively on price in conventional grocery, while plant-based milk still carries over twice the price premium of conventional milk.
The 60% retention rate on incremental gross profit is an untested assumption; if slotting and trade are heavier, the EBITDA case halves while revenue still delivers.
Holding marketing flat while adding doors risks distribution without velocity, which historically leads to delisting at the next shelf reset.
Competitor nutrition positioning, such as Silk Protein at 13g of complete plant protein, could reset shopper criteria before Oatly's door gains mature.
Expanded third-party oat capacity, including SunOpta's Modesto expansion that lifted US oat milk capacity by over 60%, supports private label and could compress branded shelf economics.
More evidence needed: no disclosed North America gross margin, so the margin improvement projection cannot be validated externally.

evidenceGaps: Oatly's current US ACV and points of distribution by channel, which determines how much door white space actually exists.
North America gross margin and SKU/customer-level profitability, needed to validate A17 and A18.
Identity, revenue share and contract term of the largest US foodservice customer, needed to size concentration risk.
2025–26 brand-level US oat milk share (Oatly versus Planet Oat, Chobani, Silk, Califia) and private-label share and price gap.
US shelf price points and promotional depth by brand and pack size, needed to set the trade spend assumption A21.
Size and profit pool of the US coffee-shop channel for oat milk, and the chain versus independent split.
US co-manufacturing capacity headroom and contract terms, to confirm incremental volume can be absorbed without capex.
Oatly US brand awareness versus trial and conversion, to test whether flat marketing can support door expansion.

executiveSummary.headline: Grow US profitably by making the coffee-shop franchise the engine of retail distribution: defend and de-concentrate foodservice, and win doors and velocity for existing Barista and core SKUs rather than launching a new portfolio.

situation.text: US retail plant-based milk is a $2.7 billion category that fell 2% in dollars and 5% in units in 2025, holding 13% of total milk dollar sales.
The decline is driven by distribution losses, not weaker demand per store: dollar velocity rose 4% and unit velocity 3% in conventional multi-outlet, and 3%/2% in natural.

Oatly is already outgrowing the category in North America: Q2 2026 revenue of $66.9M (+5.9%, volume +1.9%, price/mix +4.0%), retail up to 63% of segment revenue, and Q1 2026 retail sales +10% against a 3% oat milk decline.
North America Adjusted EBITDA has just crossed breakeven at $0.7M in Q2 2026 on higher gross profit, with group gross margin at 33.9% (+143bp) helped by a 210bp fixed-cost absorption benefit.

The coffee occasion is the defensible position: 33% of US coffee orders contain oat milk, Oatly is positioned on barista-channel dominance, and Europe & International grew volume 16.9% in a 77%-retail mix led by Barista products.

Rivals attack elsewhere — Planet Oat on price in conventional grocery, Silk on distribution and 13g-protein nutrition — while the foodservice location base shrank 8.1% to about 103,900 alt-milk-serving restaurants.

executiveSummary.recommendation: Run the Barista Bridge. Protect and de-concentrate the café franchise using the foodservice-friendly Barista SKU already sold through US distributors, then convert café-built habit into retail volume by winning club, natural and mainstream refrigerated doors for existing Barista and core SKUs — no new SKUs, no new US capacity, marketing reallocated within a flat budget. Base case: North America revenue rises from ~$258M annualised to ~$292M in 24 months with ~+200bp gross margin and ~$13M annualised segment Adjusted EBITDA (estimate), funded by trade reallocation against the $35–45M restructuring savings programme.

bullets: Defend the largest foodservice account while adding independents via distributors — excluding that customer, Q1 2026 North America grew 12.3%
Win doors at the next two shelf resets in club, natural and mainstream refrigerated (assumption: two resets in 24 months)
Reallocate flat marketing from broad awareness to café-to-home conversion and in-store visibility (assumption)
Absorb incremental volume through existing co-manufacturing under the asset-light model — no new US capacity
slides.visual: Strategy-on-a-page: café franchise → habit → retail doors → throughput → margin, with the three workstreams beneath

slides.title: Base case: ~$292M revenue and ~+200bp margin at month 24, funded by reallocation
slides.keyMessage: Growth converts to profit mainly through fixed-cost absorption on existing assets, not through added spend.
bullets: Baseline ~$258M annualised North America revenue, split ~$163M retail / ~$95M foodservice (estimate, from H1 2026 doubled at the 63% retail mix)
Base case retail +10% p.a. and foodservice flat gives ~$292M at month 24 (assumption on growth rates)
Margin improves ~200bp cumulative, scaled from the 210bp absorption benefit net of the 100bp inflation headwind (assumption)
Segment Adjusted EBITDA ~$13M annualised, assuming 60% of incremental gross profit is retained after trade and distribution (assumption)
slides.visual: Scenario bridge: baseline revenue and EBITDA to conservative / base / upside at month 24

slides.title: First 90 days: close the data gaps, then win the first wave of doors
slides.keyMessage: Do not spend against placeholder assumptions — fix the baseline in 30 days, commit in 45, execute by 90.
bullets: Days 1–30: commission US ACV and brand-share tracking; build North America margin and SKU/customer profitability; quantify foodservice concentration
Days 31–60: set door targets to the reset calendar, approve the trade envelope with a velocity hurdle, launch the independent-café distributor programme
Days 61–90: execute wave-one door wins, run the café-to-home conversion test in 2–3 metros, stand up a monthly North America margin bridge
Day 90: rebase the 24-month case for the board with validated assumptions
slides.visual: 90-day Gantt with owners, deliverables and the four decision gates marked

slides.title: The case breaks on foodservice concentration and trade cost — both are testable in 60 days
slides.keyMessage: Two unknowns carry most of the downside, and both can be resolved before major spend is committed.
bullets: Concentration: prior-year North America declines were driven mainly by sourcing changes and the segment's largest customer; share and contract term are undisclosed
Trade economics: 60% retention of incremental gross profit is untested (assumption) — if heavier, the EBITDA case roughly halves
Structural headwinds: alt-milk-serving locations -8.1%; category units -5% while prices rose 2%
Competitive resets: Silk Protein at 13g and expanded third-party capacity supporting private label could compress branded shelf economics
slides.visual: Risk heat map (impact versus evidence confidence) with the 60-day mitigation or test beside each risk

slides.title: Evidence gaps to close before committing year-two spend
slides.keyMessage: Five disclosures would move the plan from a defensible direction to a costed commitment.
bullets: More evidence needed: Oatly US ACV and points of distribution by channel — sizes the actual door white space
More evidence needed: North America gross margin and SKU/customer profitability — validates the margin and retention assumptions
More evidence needed: largest US foodservice customer revenue share and contract status — sizes concentration risk
More evidence needed: 2025–26 brand-level US oat milk shares, private-label price gap and 2026 shelf prices by pack size
slides.visual: Gap register: question, owner, source, decision it unblocks, due date

slides.title: Decisions requested today
slides.keyMessage: Approve the direction and the 90-day diagnostic; defer the trade envelope to Day 45.
bullets: Approve the Barista Bridge as the US direction for 24 months, with no new US capacity and flat marketing
Approve the ~$1–2M one-off commercial analytics build to close the ACV, share and margin gaps (assumption on cost)
Agree the foodservice posture will be set at Day 60 on the basis of the concentration memo
Agree the trigger to shift toward a margin-first posture if North America Adjusted EBITDA falls back to breakeven
